youtube.title: Leaning Tower of Pisa: Why Didn't It Fall Over?
youtube.description:
The Leaning Tower of Pisa should have fallen 800 years ago, and a war is the reason it didn't.

Work began in 1173, and within five years the tower was sinking into soft clay on a shallow foundation. Then Pisa went to war with Genoa, Lucca and Florence, and building stopped for almost a century. That long pause let the clay settle and firm up; engineers say that without it, the tower would almost certainly have toppled. When work restarted, the builders made the upper floors taller on the low side, so the Pisa tower is not just tilted, it's curved like a banana.

Subscribe to Stickstory for a strange true story like this every day. Would you climb a tower that leans? Tell me in the comments!

scenes.text: A war saved the Leaning Tower.
scenes.visual: Hook frame in the Piazza of Pisa: the white marble tower stands big in the middle, leaning right and creaking a little further over, the pale cathedral behind on the left, green lawn and a marble path in front; on 'war' a spear with a red Pisan war banner springs up out of the lawn at the right edge; the fez host appears big bottom-left in shock as the cover overlay.

scenes.text: Building began in 1173. Five years on, it was sinking into soft clay.
scenes.visual: Cutaway of the ground under Pisa: layers of sand and grey hatched clay down to the frame bottom; a white marble stump on a shallow stone slab rises storey by storey inside a wooden scaffold; on 'sinking' it sinks into the clay and tips to the right, the clay layers bending down under it; red card '1173', hand label 'SOFT CLAY'.

scenes.text: Then Pisa went to war, and work stopped for nearly a century.
scenes.visual: A hillside: the leaning three-storey stump stands abandoned in its scaffold left of centre while soldiers in grey iron helmets with spears and red banners with a pale cross march past behind it, and a near row of big soldiers marches the other way across the bottom of the frame; on 'stopped' a big red year counter runs from 1178 to 1272 and green vines creep up the stump; hand card 'ALMOST 100 YEARS'.

scenes.text: Here's the twist: the pause let the clay firm up.
scenes.visual: Close-up of the cutaway: the overgrown stump in its scaffold on the sunken slab; the fez host stands on the ground at the left and points down into the clay; from 'pause' the hatched clay layers squeeze tighter and darker while water drops rise out of them to the surface; blue card 'FIRMER'.

scenes.text: Without it, the tower would almost surely have fallen.
scenes.visual: What-if in red ink: a ghost tower keeps rising storey after storey on the soft clay with no pause; as 'fallen' is spoken it cracks and topples over to the right until it lies almost flat, the clay sags under it and dust bursts where it lands; red card 'NO PAUSE?' top right.

scenes.text: When work restarted, builders made the upper floors taller on the low side.
scenes.visual: Work restarts: close-up on the top of the tower inside its scaffold: new marble storeys drop into place one by one, each a wedge that is taller on the right, low side; a mason in a beret stands on a plank holding a column, then points at the new storey; on 'low' red measure marks show the new storey's short left and long right side, and a thick red arrow points at the taller side with the card 'TALLER!'.

scenes.text: So today it's not just tilted.
scenes.visual: The finished tower in the Piazza today; two tourists on the lawn at the left do the classic 'holding it up' pose with their arms raised; on 'tilted' a red dashed plumb line drops from the top down to the ground, far from the base; red card 'ABOUT 4°'.
The whole tower: from 'bent' a thick gold line traces its axis from base to top and curves back, next to a straight dashed line; on 'banana' a big ink banana pops up on the right.

scenes.text: Subscribe for one strange true story a day.
scenes.visual: The Piazza: the fez host stands at the foot of the tower with his hand against its marble base, pushing it up like a tourist, then on 'story' turns and points at the viewer.
